transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, what brings me in is… it’s kind of embarrassing, actually. I’ve been noticing that when people are talking directly to me, like at the museum when we’re discussing the next art walk, I’ll be looking right at them and nodding along, and then suddenly I realize I missed the whole middle part of what they said. Not because I don’t care—I do care—but it’s like my mind slips off somewhere for a moment.

Then I have to ask them to repeat it, like, “Could you run that by me again?” And after a while I feel awkward, because it’s not like they were across the room or mumbling. They were right there in front of me. So I guess I’m here because that keeps happening, and I’d like to understand why.
Do these moments where your mind slips away tend to happen more often when you're feeling stressed or anxious?

I mean… I haven’t really sorted out whether it’s stress exactly. It happens in pretty ordinary situations too, like at the museum when we’re talking about the next art walk. Someone will be speaking right to me, and I’ll be looking at them, nodding like I’m following, and then all of a sudden I realize I didn’t catch the middle of what they said.

And then I have to say, “Sorry, could you run that by me again?” It’s not that I’m panicking in that moment or anything. It’s more like my attention just sort of drifts off without me noticing, and by the time I notice, I’ve missed a chunk of it. So stress might make it worse, maybe, but I can’t say it only happens when I’m anxious.
Do you have trouble remembering things that happened earlier in the day or things that people told you outside of these moments when your mind slips away?

I’m not really sure how to separate that out, to be honest. I mean, I don’t think of myself as someone who just can’t remember the day or anything like that. If something happened earlier, I usually have some sense of it.

But with things people tell me… that’s harder to answer, because sometimes if I don’t remember it later, I don’t always know whether I forgot it after hearing it, or whether I never really took it in properly in the first place. Like, if someone says, “Remember I told you this?” I may think, well, maybe you did, but maybe that was one of those times where I was looking like I was listening and I missed part of it.

So outside of those moments, I haven’t especially noticed a separate memory problem, if that makes sense. It feels more like the trouble starts at the point of taking in what’s being said.
Do you feel anything physically, like a sensation in your body, when your mind slips away and you miss part of what someone is saying?

I don’t think so… not that I’ve noticed, anyway. It’s not like I feel dizzy or my heart starts racing or I get a tightness in my chest right when it happens. At least, I haven’t connected it with anything like that.

It’s more that afterward I sort of “come back,” if that’s the right way to put it, and realize I’ve missed something. Then I feel awkward or a little embarrassed because the person was talking right to me and I was acting like I was following. But physically, during the slipping-away part, I can’t say there’s a specific sensation I recognize. If there is, it’s subtle enough that I haven’t really picked up on it.
Do you ever find yourself zoning out or missing parts of what you're reading or watching, similar to what happens when you're listening to someone?

Yes, that happens too. Reading is probably the easiest example for me to notice, because there’s a page right in front of me showing that I didn’t really take it in.

Like, if I sit down with a gallery packet, or some notes about an exhibit or an upcoming art walk, I’ll start out okay. I’ll be reading the first paragraph or two and thinking, alright, I’m following this. But then after a few minutes my eyes are still going across the page, line by line, and it looks like I’m reading, but my mind has gone somewhere else. Then I get to the bottom of a section and realize I don’t actually know what I just read.

So I’ll go back and read the same part again. Sometimes I have to do that more than once, which gets a little frustrating because it’s not usually that the material is impossible or anything. It’s more like I didn’t stay with it long enough for it to land. Watching something can be similar, but with reading I notice it more clearly because I catch myself rereading the same few lines.
Do you ever find yourself zoning out or losing focus when you're doing tasks that require your full attention, like working on a project or during conversations with multiple people?

Yes, I do, especially with things like reading through a gallery packet or a set of notes where I really do need to take it in. I’ll sit down and start out perfectly fine — like the first little bit, I’m with it, I understand what I’m reading, I know why I’m looking at it.

But then after a few minutes, it’s like my eyes keep doing the job but my mind doesn’t. I’m still moving across the page, line by line, and if someone looked at me they’d probably think I was reading carefully. But then I get to the end of a paragraph or a section and realize, wait, I don’t actually know what I just read.

So I have to go back and read the same part again, sometimes more than once. It’s frustrating because I’m not trying to avoid it, and it’s not that I can’t understand the material. It’s more like my attention just doesn’t stay attached to it long enough.
Do you feel anxious or upset right before your mind slips away and you miss part of what someone is saying?

Not really right before, no. I wouldn’t say I feel anxious first and then drift off. It’s more the other way around, I think — I’m at the museum, someone is talking directly to me about the next art walk or something we’re planning, and I’m looking at them like I’m listening. I’m not upset in that moment, not that I can tell.

Then all of a sudden I realize I missed the middle of what they said. Like I caught the beginning, and maybe I catch the end, but there’s this gap where I don’t really know how we got from one point to the next. That’s when I get uncomfortable, because I have to say, “I’m sorry, can you run that by me again?” And I don’t like doing that, especially if they were explaining something pretty straightforward.

So the anxious or embarrassed feeling is more after I notice I missed it, not before. Beforehand it just kind of happens.
Do you find it difficult to focus when you're alone, like when you're trying to work on a project by yourself?

Yes, definitely when I’m alone too. In some ways it’s easier to notice then, because there isn’t another person there keeping me on track.

Like if I sit down with a gallery packet or a set of notes, I can start out fine. I’ll think, okay, I’m just going to read through this and get what I need from it. And for the first few minutes I usually do. But then my eyes are still moving over the page, like I’m reading each line, and my mind has kind of wandered off somewhere else without me realizing it.

Then I get to the end of a paragraph or a section and I have that moment of, “Wait, what did I just read?” And I’ll have to go back and read the same part again. Sometimes it’s not even that the material is hard — it’s just that I didn’t really stay with it. That can happen even when I’m by myself and there’s nothing especially dramatic going on around me.
Have you noticed that these episodes of zoning out or missing parts of conversations are affecting your relationships or work in any significant way?

Yes… I think it has, though I don’t always like admitting that, because I’ve been involved with the museum group for a long time and I used to feel pretty steady with it.

It’s not like anyone has sat me down and said, “You can’t handle this,” or anything harsh like that. It’s been more subtle. Some of the planning pieces — like keeping track of what needs to be discussed for an art walk, or following through on little details from a meeting — those have sort of quietly shifted away from me. Someone else will take the lead on that part now, or they’ll say, “Oh, I’ve got this,” and I can tell it’s partly because I’ve missed things or needed things repeated.

And that does affect how I feel leading the art walks. I used to feel confident being out front, talking through the pieces and keeping the flow going. Now I second-guess myself more. I worry I’m going to miss something someone told me, or forget part of the plan, or not be as on top of it as I should be. So I still care about it, very much, but I don’t feel as reliable in that role as I used to.
How much distress or upset do you feel about these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

It bothers me, yes. I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart over it every day, but it does upset me more than I probably let on.

The hardest part is that it’s changed how I feel in the museum group. That’s been a place where I used to feel useful and, you know, like I had my part. But because I miss pieces of conversations or don’t catch all the details, some of the planning things have sort of been moved away from me. Not in a mean way — nobody has been cruel about it — but I notice it. Someone else will step in to handle a detail, or they’ll kind of take over the organizing part, and I’m left thinking, “Well, they probably don’t trust me with that like they used to.”

And leading the art walks… that’s where I feel it emotionally. I used to feel pretty confident doing that. Now I get this nagging feeling that I’m going to miss something important or not be as sharp as I should be. So the upset is not constant panic or anything like that, but it’s discouraging. It makes me feel less capable than I used to feel.
Are you having trouble completing everyday tasks because of these episodes of zoning out?

Yes, some. Not every single day, and I do eventually get things done most of the time, but the follow-through is where I notice it.

For example, with the volunteer group, someone might give me a few things to handle before an art walk. And I’ll start out doing it — like I’ll print the maps, and I’ll feel like, okay, I’m on it. But then the next part, like calling the museum desk or making sure the folders are completely ready, can just sort of slip away from me. It’s not that I decided not to do it. It’s more like I did the first piece and my brain treated that as if the whole task was finished.

Then later someone will ask, “Did you call the desk?” or “Are the folders ready?” and I’ll realize they’re only half-ready, or I never made the call. That’s embarrassing, because these are ordinary things. They’re not complicated. But if there are several steps, especially if nobody checks in, I can lose track after the first part and need a reminder.
Are these episodes of zoning out affecting your daily routine in a significant way?

Yes, I’d say it does, though maybe not in the sense of, you know, I can’t get through a normal day at home. It’s more that the things that give structure to my week — especially the museum group — have changed because of it.

I’ve noticed that some of the planning parts have sort of quietly been taken off my plate. Nobody makes a big announcement about it, but I can tell. If there’s something that needs organizing before an art walk, someone else will step in or handle the details now, where before I would’ve been trusted to keep track of it. And I understand why, because I have missed pieces of conversations or not followed through the way I meant to, but it still stings.

And with leading the art walks, that’s probably where it affects my routine the most emotionally. I still show up, and I still care about doing it well, but I don’t feel confident the way I used to. I find myself worrying that I’m going to miss part of what was planned or not have the flow right. So yes, it’s significant to me — maybe mild compared to some people, but in my daily life, or at least my regular week, it has definitely made me feel less steady and less useful than before.
How long have you been experiencing these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

It’s been, let me think… a little over two years now. About two years and four months, I’d say, where it really started causing trouble and wasn’t just the occasional “oh, I missed that” kind of thing.

It was after my friend died. He and I had both been involved with the museum things, and after he was gone I took over the liaison duties by myself. That’s when I noticed it more clearly, because there wasn’t someone beside me catching the details or helping carry the conversation. I’d be in meetings or planning talks, and I’d miss pieces, and then later realize I hadn’t really taken in everything I needed to.

So I might have had little moments before that, I suppose, but the noticeable problem — the part that’s actually been interfering — has been since then, about two years and four months.
You mentioned that these episodes started after your friend died, do you think there's a connection between his death and when you first noticed these symptoms?

Yes, I think there probably is a connection, at least in terms of when I really noticed it. I don’t know if his death caused it exactly, but that’s when it started being a problem I couldn’t brush off.

Before that, he and I sort of shared the museum liaison things, and he would catch details or remember parts of conversations that I might not have held onto. After he died, I was doing those duties by myself, and that’s when it became obvious that I was missing pieces and not keeping track the way I needed to.

So the timing is pretty clear to me: it’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since he died and I took over that role alone.
Have you noticed any changes in your social relationships due to these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

Yes, I have noticed it some, mostly with the people at the museum. That’s really what made me feel like I needed to come in, honestly.

They’ll be talking right to me — not across the room, not in some noisy situation necessarily — but right to me about the next art walk, like who’s doing what, where we’re starting, what needs to be mentioned. And I’ll be looking at them, nodding even, feeling like I’m following along. Then all of a sudden I realize I missed the middle part of what they said. It’s embarrassing, because from the outside I probably look like I’m listening, but inside it’s like there’s a blank spot.

So I have to say, “I’m sorry, can you run that by me again?” And people are usually polite about it, but after a while you can feel the patience wearing thin, or maybe I’m imagining some of that, but it changes the feeling between us. I don’t feel as reliable in those conversations as I used to. It makes me a little more hesitant socially, because I worry I’m going to miss something important and make someone repeat themselves again.
Are you feeling like you're withdrawing from social interactions or responsibilities because of these episodes of zoning out?

Yes… I think I am, a bit. I don’t know that I’d say I’ve pulled away completely, because I still care about the museum group and I still show up, but I’m not stepping into things the way I used to.

What’s happened is, some of the planning pieces have sort of been moved away from me. Not in a dramatic way — nobody sat me down and said, “You can’t handle this anymore” — but I’ve noticed that other people will take over certain details now, or they’ll make the final arrangements without relying on me as much. And honestly, I can’t entirely blame them, because if I miss part of a conversation, then something can fall through the cracks.

The harder part for me is the art walks. I used to feel pretty comfortable leading them, keeping the flow going, remembering what needed to be said and who was involved. Lately I don’t feel as confident doing that. I worry I’ll miss an instruction or forget some planning point someone told me, and then I’ll be standing there responsible for everyone and not quite have the full picture.

So yes, I guess I have backed off some — partly because others have quietly shifted things away from me, and partly because I don’t trust myself in those responsibilities the way I used to.
Are you feeling like these episodes are affecting your overall quality of life?

Yes, I would say it’s affecting my quality of life, even if it’s not like my whole life has collapsed or anything. It’s more that it’s taken away some of the confidence I had in the parts of my life that mattered to me.

The museum group has been a big part of my routine and my sense of usefulness, I guess. And now, because I miss things or don’t hold onto parts of conversations the way I should, some of the planning pieces have kind of been shifted away from me. Quietly, not in a harsh way, but I notice it. People will handle certain arrangements themselves, or they won’t depend on me for the details the way they used to.

And the art walks especially… I used to feel comfortable leading those. I liked being able to guide people through, keep things moving, feel like I knew what was supposed to happen. Now I don’t feel that same confidence. I worry I won’t have the full picture, or that I’ll miss something someone told me and then I’ll be the one standing there trying to lead without really knowing what I’m supposed to remember.

So yes, it affects me. Maybe mildly compared to what some people deal with, but for me it’s been a real loss of confidence and independence in something that used to feel like my place.
Have you been experiencing these episodes of zoning out for more than 6 months?

Yes, definitely more than six months. The time I can put my finger on is about two years and four months now.

It really became noticeable after my friend died and I ended up taking over the museum liaison duties by myself. Before that, maybe I had little moments here and there like anyone does, but it wasn’t causing real trouble in the same way. Once I was the one responsible for keeping track of more of the details on my own, that’s when the zoning out and missing pieces of conversations started to matter, and I started noticing it as an actual problem.

So yes — not just a recent thing. It’s been going on long enough that I can look back and say it’s been affecting me for a couple of years now.
Have you been experiencing these episodes of zoning out for at least 6 months without any significant improvement?

Yes… yes, it’s definitely been at least six months without it really improving. I know I mentioned the time frame already, but the best marker for me is still when my friend died and I took over the museum liaison duties by myself. That was about two years and four months ago.

Since then, it’s been noticeably causing trouble. It hasn’t been one of those things where I had a bad month and then got back to normal. I keep thinking maybe I’ll settle into it or get used to the responsibilities, but the zoning out and missing parts of things has stayed around enough that it still affects me. So, yes — more than six months, and I wouldn’t say there’s been any significant improvement.
Have you experienced significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to these episodes of zoning out for most of the past 6 months?

Yes, I think so. I mean, I wouldn’t say it has ruined everything, but it has definitely impaired things that matter to me.

The museum group is the clearest example. There are planning pieces that I used to be trusted with, or at least that I felt I was part of, and over time some of those have been quietly shifted away from me. Nobody has been cruel about it, and that almost makes it harder to talk about, because it’s subtle. It’s more like someone else will take care of the arrangements, or they’ll double-check things without really saying why, or they just won’t put me in charge of the details the way they used to.

And with the art walks, that’s where I feel it emotionally. I used to feel confident leading them. I knew what I was doing, I felt useful, I felt like I had a role. Now I second-guess myself before and during them, because I worry I’ve missed something or that I won’t remember part of what was discussed. So I don’t feel as steady leading them as I used to.

So yes, for most of the past six months, it’s caused distress and some impairment — maybe mild in the big picture, but real for me.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the attention problems are causing significant impact on relationships or work/functioning, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it has, though I don’t always like admitting that, because I’ve been involved with the museum group for a long time and I used to feel pretty steady with it.

It’s not like anyone has sat me down and said, “You can’t handle this,” or anything harsh like that. It’s been more subtle. Some of the planning pieces — like keeping track of what needs to be discussed for an art walk, or following through on little details from a meeting — those have sort of quietly shifted away from me. Someone else will take the lead on that part now, or they’ll say, “Oh, I’ve got this,” and I can tell it’s partly because I’ve missed things or needed things repeated.

And that does affect how I feel leading the art walks. I used to feel confident being out front, talking through the pieces and keeping the flow going. Now I second-guess myself more. I worry I’m going to miss something someone told me, or forget part of the plan, or not be as on top of it as I should be. So I still care about it, very much, but I don’t feel as reliable in that role as I used to.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress
doctor.question: How much distress or upset do you feel about these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the degree of distress or upset caused by the zoning out and missed conversations, which is most directly related to the impact these symptoms have on the patient's functioning and confidence.

patient.answer:
It bothers me, yes. I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart over it every day, but it does upset me more than I probably let on.

The hardest part is that it’s changed how I feel in the museum group. That’s been a place where I used to feel useful and, you know, like I had my part. But because I miss pieces of conversations or don’t catch all the details, some of the planning things have sort of been moved away from me. Not in a mean way — nobody has been cruel about it — but I notice it. Someone else will step in to handle a detail, or they’ll kind of take over the organizing part, and I’m left thinking, “Well, they probably don’t trust me with that like they used to.”

And leading the art walks… that’s where I feel it emotionally. I used to feel pretty confident doing that. Now I get this nagging feeling that I’m going to miss something important or not be as sharp as I should be. So the upset is not constant panic or anything like that, but it’s discouraging. It makes me feel less capable than I used to feel.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting daily life
doctor.question: Are you having trouble completing everyday tasks because of these episodes of zoning out?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When someone gives me a few things to handle for the volunteer group, I’ll do the first part, like printing the maps, but then I may forget to call the museum desk or leave the folders half-ready until someone reminds me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about difficulty completing everyday tasks, which directly matches problems following through and finishing duties.

patient.answer:
Yes, some. Not every single day, and I do eventually get things done most of the time, but the follow-through is where I notice it.

For example, with the volunteer group, someone might give me a few things to handle before an art walk. And I’ll start out doing it — like I’ll print the maps, and I’ll feel like, okay, I’m on it. But then the next part, like calling the museum desk or making sure the folders are completely ready, can just sort of slip away from me. It’s not that I decided not to do it. It’s more like I did the first piece and my brain treated that as if the whole task was finished.

Then later someone will ask, “Did you call the desk?” or “Are the folders ready?” and I’ll realize they’re only half-ready, or I never made the call. That’s embarrassing, because these are ordinary things. They’re not complicated. But if there are several steps, especially if nobody checks in, I can lose track after the first part and need a reminder.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting daily life
doctor.question: Are these episodes of zoning out affecting your daily routine in a significant way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the zoning out significantly affects the patient's daily routine, which is most directly about functional impairment in daily activities and roles.

patient.answer:
Yes, I’d say it does, though maybe not in the sense of, you know, I can’t get through a normal day at home. It’s more that the things that give structure to my week — especially the museum group — have changed because of it.

I’ve noticed that some of the planning parts have sort of quietly been taken off my plate. Nobody makes a big announcement about it, but I can tell. If there’s something that needs organizing before an art walk, someone else will step in or handle the details now, where before I would’ve been trusted to keep track of it. And I understand why, because I have missed pieces of conversations or not followed through the way I meant to, but it still stings.

And with leading the art walks, that’s probably where it affects my routine the most emotionally. I still show up, and I still care about doing it well, but I don’t feel confident the way I used to. I find myself worrying that I’m going to miss part of what was planned or not have the flow right. So yes, it’s significant to me — maybe mild compared to some people, but in my daily life, or at least my regular week, it has definitely made me feel less steady and less useful than before.

doctor.intent: determine if symptoms are persistent over time
doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since my friend died and I took over the museum liaison duties by myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the zoning out and missed conversation episodes have been occurring, which directly corresponds to the duration item.

patient.answer:
It’s been, let me think… a little over two years now. About two years and four months, I’d say, where it really started causing trouble and wasn’t just the occasional “oh, I missed that” kind of thing.

It was after my friend died. He and I had both been involved with the museum things, and after he was gone I took over the liaison duties by myself. That’s when I noticed it more clearly, because there wasn’t someone beside me catching the details or helping carry the conversation. I’d be in meetings or planning talks, and I’d miss pieces, and then later realize I hadn’t really taken in everything I needed to.

So I might have had little moments before that, I suppose, but the noticeable problem — the part that’s actually been interfering — has been since then, about two years and four months.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are related to a traumatic event
doctor.question: You mentioned that these episodes started after your friend died, do you think there's a connection between his death and when you first noticed these symptoms?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since my friend died and I took over the museum liaison duties by myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is about the timing of symptom onset in relation to the friend's death, which is covered by the duration item.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think there probably is a connection, at least in terms of when I really noticed it. I don’t know if his death caused it exactly, but that’s when it started being a problem I couldn’t brush off.

Before that, he and I sort of shared the museum liaison things, and he would catch details or remember parts of conversations that I might not have held onto. After he died, I was doing those duties by myself, and that’s when it became obvious that I was missing pieces and not keeping track the way I needed to.

So the timing is pretty clear to me: it’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since he died and I took over that role alone.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their social relationships
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your social relationships due to these episodes of zoning out and missing parts of conversations?

target_item.name: Listening_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that people at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk, and I’ll be looking at them, but then I realize I missed the middle of what they said and have to ask them to run it by me again.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of zoning out and missing parts of conversations, which most directly relates to difficulty listening when spoken to directly.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have noticed it some, mostly with the people at the museum. That’s really what made me feel like I needed to come in, honestly.

They’ll be talking right to me — not across the room, not in some noisy situation necessarily — but right to me about the next art walk, like who’s doing what, where we’re starting, what needs to be mentioned. And I’ll be looking at them, nodding even, feeling like I’m following along. Then all of a sudden I realize I missed the middle part of what they said. It’s embarrassing, because from the outside I probably look like I’m listening, but inside it’s like there’s a blank spot.

So I have to say, “I’m sorry, can you run that by me again?” And people are usually polite about it, but after a while you can feel the patience wearing thin, or maybe I’m imagining some of that, but it changes the feeling between us. I don’t feel as reliable in those conversations as I used to. It makes me a little more hesitant socially, because I worry I’m going to miss something important and make someone repeat themselves again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you feeling like you're withdrawing from social interactions or responsibilities because of these episodes of zoning out?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the zoning out is leading to withdrawal from social interactions or responsibilities, which is most directly about impairment in functioning and reduced confidence or participation in museum duties.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I am, a bit. I don’t know that I’d say I’ve pulled away completely, because I still care about the museum group and I still show up, but I’m not stepping into things the way I used to.

What’s happened is, some of the planning pieces have sort of been moved away from me. Not in a dramatic way — nobody sat me down and said, “You can’t handle this anymore” — but I’ve noticed that other people will take over certain details now, or they’ll make the final arrangements without relying on me as much. And honestly, I can’t entirely blame them, because if I miss part of a conversation, then something can fall through the cracks.

The harder part for me is the art walks. I used to feel pretty comfortable leading them, keeping the flow going, remembering what needed to be said and who was involved. Lately I don’t feel as confident doing that. I worry I’ll miss an instruction or forget some planning point someone told me, and then I’ll be standing there responsible for everyone and not quite have the full picture.

So yes, I guess I have backed off some — partly because others have quietly shifted things away from me, and partly because I don’t trust myself in those responsibilities the way I used to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you feeling like these episodes are affecting your overall quality of life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: The museum group has had to quietly shift some planning pieces away from me, and I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to.

patient.answer:
Yes, I would say it’s affecting my quality of life, even if it’s not like my whole life has collapsed or anything. It’s more that it’s taken away some of the confidence I had in the parts of my life that mattered to me.

The museum group has been a big part of my routine and my sense of usefulness, I guess. And now, because I miss things or don’t hold onto parts of conversations the way I should, some of the planning pieces have kind of been shifted away from me. Quietly, not in a harsh way, but I notice it. People will handle certain arrangements themselves, or they won’t depend on me for the details the way they used to.

And the art walks especially… I used to feel comfortable leading those. I liked being able to guide people through, keep things moving, feel like I knew what was supposed to happen. Now I don’t feel that same confidence. I worry I won’t have the full picture, or that I’ll miss something someone told me and then I’ll be the one standing there trying to lead without really knowing what I’m supposed to remember.

So yes, it affects me. Maybe mildly compared to what some people deal with, but for me it’s been a real loss of confidence and independence in something that used to feel like my place.
